title: Should leaders be licensed?
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez opens with a thought experiment about an untrained billing clerk filling in as a therapist, then turns it on managers. Therapists need degrees, supervised practice and licensure because they affect others' well-being, yet supervisors with arguably more influence on well-being are handed teams with no training or standards. She insists leadership is mostly about how you show up for people, and that leaders are made, not born. Neglecting the emotional impact of leaders on their teams is negligent, she argues, because talent leaves, burnout spreads and culture decays. Her closing move is to treat leadership as a discipline and craft deserving support, training and higher standards.
points: Promotion into management is handed out casually, with no training, supervision or standards, unlike professions that shape well-being.
Supervisors affect employee well-being as much as or more than therapists, which links to retention and productivity.
Leadership is mainly about relationships, communication, trust and culture rather than budgets and tasks.
Untrained leaders cause burnout, attrition and cultural rot, so organisations should treat leadership as a craft that is taught.
quotes: But arguably, supervisors have more direct impact on their team members’ mental health than therapists do. Even the Society for Human Resource Management reports this to be true (good work, SHRM!).
Nada. No license required. Heck, not even training is required. We hand out supervisory responsibilities like we hand out party favors.

Leadership is significantly less about budgets, projects, and tasks than it is about how you show up for people. It’s about navigating human relationships. About fostering communication, cultivating trust, and building culture—all skills that profoundly impact the well-being of every team member, and that of the company overall.

Like good leaders, good therapists are also made, not born. The difference? Therapy (as a profession) knows this. As such, anyone looking to become a therapist has no choice but to go through a series of rigorous coursework and training. Years of education, hundreds of hours of clinical training, supervised practice, licensing exams—the whole nine yards.
A leader may chart the course, but the team takes the journey. The team takes the idea, the blueprint, the vision, and turns it into magic.
When people are hurt by the aftershock of thoughtless or unintentional leadership, talent bleeds, burnout spreads, and cultures rot.
